'''John W. Drake''' (February 10, 1932 – February 2, 2020) was an [[United States of America|American]] [[microbiologist]] and [[geneticist]], working for over half a century in the field of [[mutagenesis]] and [[DNA repair]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.genetics.org/content/216/4/827 |title=John W. (Jan) Drake: A Biochemical View of a Geneticist Par Excellence |last1=Reha-Krantz |first1=Linda J. |last2=Goodman |first2= Myron F. |date=2020-12-01 |work=[[Genetics_(journal)]] |access-date=2020-03-08 |language=en}}</ref>

==Education and early career==
His interest in [[embryology]] led him to take his PhD at the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1958<ref name="niehs">{{cite web
 |url         = http://www.niehs.nih.gov/research/atniehs/labs/lmg/smdnar/index.cfm
 |title       = Spontaneous Mutation & DNA Repair Group
 |publisher   = [[National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences|NIEHS]]
 |access-date  = December 18, 2010
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20101220181850/http://www.niehs.nih.gov/research/atniehs/labs/lmg/smdnar/index.cfm
 |archive-date = December 20, 2010
 |df          = dmy-all
}}</ref> where he studied alongside [[Howard Temin]] in the laboratory of [[Renato Dulbecco]].<ref>{{cite journal
|first1=John W.
|last1=Drake

|pmc=1207483

|doi=10.1093/genetics/144.1.1
}}</ref>

==Research interests and career==
Based on earlier observations on the mutation frequencies of the [[T4 phage|bacteriophage T4]], Drake in the early 1960s began to study the biochemical activities of the [[DNA polymerase|T4 polymerase]]. For this, he established a phage genetics laboratory at the [[University of Illinois]]. Together with his coworkers he could dissect both pro- and anti-mutagenic activities of the T4 DNA polymerases during [[viral replication]]. To describe the mutation rate in a quantitative way for different organisms, Drake postulated that the mutation rate (per base position and per replication cycle) is proportional to the total genome size of a DNA-based microorganism ("Drakes Law").<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.pnas.org/content/88/16/7160.long |title=A constant rate of spontaneous mutation in DNA-based microbes. |last=Drake |first=John W. |date=1991-08-15 |work=[[PNAS]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |url=https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1749-6632.1999.tb08870.x?sid=nlm%3Apubmed |title=The distribution of rates of spontaneous mutation over viruses, prokaryotes, and eukaryotes   |last=Drake |first=John W. |date=1999-05-18 |journal=[[Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences]] |volume=870 |issue=1 |pages=100–107 |doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.1999.tb08870.x |pmid=10415476 |bibcode=1999NYASA.870..100D |s2cid=45542650 |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His own discovery of mutator phenotypes (i.e. bacterial or phage strains which display an exceptionally high mutation rate), however demonstrated that there can be deviations (hypermutability) from this general rule.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.genetics.org/content/86/3/501.long |title=Mutator mutations in bacteriophage T4 gene 42 (dHMC hydroxymethylase) |last1=Williams |first1=W.E. |last2=Drake |first2=J.W. |date=1977-07-25 |work=[[Genetics_(journal)]] |language=en}}</ref>

As an early member of the [[Environmental Mutagen Society]], John W. Drake chaired its "Committee 17"  which published an influential position paper; “Environmental Mutagenic Hazards”, in [[Science (journal)|Science]] in 1975.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Environmental Mutagenic Hazards |journal=Science |date=February 14, 1975 |volume=187 |pages=503–514 |doi=10.1126/science.163482|issue=4176|pmid=163482 |bibcode=1975Sci...187..503. }}</ref> This described the research needs and regulatory responsibility for managing potential mutagenic compounds in the environment. It significantly influenced research direction, regulatory procedures and mutagenicity testing within industry within the United States and internationally.<ref name="ems">{{cite web|url=http://www.ems-us.org/|title=Environmental Mutagen Society web site|access-date=December 12, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110416011023/http://www.ems-us.org/|archive-date=April 16, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> 

Later, he pioneered research on the mutational processes during replication of RNA viruses and RNA bacteriophages.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Rates of spontaneous mutation among RNA viruses  |last=Drake |first=John W. |date=1993-05-01 |work=[[PNAS]] |volume=90 |issue=9 |pages=4171–5 |doi=10.1073/pnas.90.9.4171 |pmid=8387212 |pmc=46468 |language=en|doi-access=free }}</ref> Results from these studies had far reaching consequences for the understanding of the mechanisms that drive viral evolution of human pathogens such as [[Influenza A virus]], [[Hepatitis C virus]] and [[SARS coronavirus 2]].

As editor-in-chief of [[Genetics_(journal)|GENETICS]] from 1982 to 1996, Jan Drake helped to make the journal a first-choice for scientific publications from all over the world.  
In the last years of his academic and scientific career, John W. Drake headed the Spontaneous Mutation and DNA Repair Group within the Laboratory of Molecular Genetics at the [[National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences]].<ref name="niehs" />
He was fellow of the [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]].
